A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LINVIDEO work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. V1 ends with references despite referring to an appendix; v2 includes Appendix A–H. The supplied contents support reliable comparison of what each version documents.

before.justification: V1 reports original Wan1.3B generation-quality evaluations, inference and training timings, and layer-selection and objective ablations in Section 5.

after.justification: V2 retains original Wan1.3B experiments, adds Wan14B benchmark and latency results, and includes numerical ablations and generated examples in its appendix.

M1.justification: The Hedgehog kernel, learnable layer-selection scores, constraint and regularization losses, ADM objective, score estimator, and optional subsequent DMD2 distillation remain unchanged. Applying the framework to Wan14B and documenting the existing two-stage procedure do not introduce a new proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions study text-to-video generation using synthetic model trajectories and evaluate VBench and VBench-2.0. OpenVid is newly disclosed as the prompt source, without evidence of a dataset replacement. Model size, resolution and frame-count differences concern experimental configurations within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparators remain FlashAttention2, DFA, XAttention, SVG and SVG2; the Manual, Heuristic and objective controls also remain. Appendix F quantifies the direct-distillation failure already reported qualitatively in v1 Section 4.3. SLA receives an explicit exclusion explanation but is not evaluated in either version.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 adds a substantial configuration: Wan14B at 720p, replacing 22/40 attention layers and training on 32 H100 GPUs, alongside the retained Wan1.3B configuration. Appendix C specifies annealed and fixed-alpha comparison settings. Conversely, v1 Figure 7's latency sweep over 81, 161 and 321 frames is removed. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: The appendix supplies alpha-schedule sensitivity results, visual evidence of temporal jitter under the naive objective, and a quantitative comparison of direct versus sequential distillation and linearization. Several questions were mentioned in v1, but their supporting appendix evidence was absent. V2 also removes the frame-length scaling analysis from v1 Figure 7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. Appendix A's videos-per-prompt counts disclose evaluation sample sizes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The Wan1.3B quality scores in Tables 1–4 are retained. V2 adds Wan14B results, including 1127-second inference at 1.71× speedup and 92.56-second distilled inference at 20.9×, plus VBench-2.0 totals of 59.62 and 58.22 respectively. Appendix Tables I–II add alpha-ablation and direct-distillation scores, while the longer-frame latency results disappear. These are additional or removed results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds the previously unavailable derivation of Equation (13), starting from the general score–velocity relationship, substituting the rectified-flow schedules and subtracting the two scores. The main equations and formal assumptions remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary replace the 1.25–2.00× acceleration claim with 1.43–1.71× and expand the distilled-model claim from 15.92× to 15.9–20.9×. These ranges reflect different reported configuration coverage. The central data-free post-training, selective-transfer and ADM contributions remain the same.

C2.justification: Appendices B–C explain how alpha changes the regularizer's gradient landscape and interpret the new ablation as supporting schedule robustness. Appendix F makes the training-stability rationale for sequential linearization and distillation explicit. These extend the interpretation without changing the main mechanism claims or introducing a substantially different applicability boundary.

D1.justification: Appendices A and G disclose the OpenVid prompt source, 81-frame inputs with 21 latent frames, FSDP, 10% warm-up, batch sizes 48/64, initial learning rate 0.0001, alpha decay from 20 to 2, and the 128-prompt heuristic-selection procedure. Evaluation counts of five videos per VBench prompt and three or twenty per VBench-2.0 prompt are also supplied. These substantially improve reproducibility, chiefly through additional disclosure.

R1.justification: V2 shortens the early-video survey and removes citations including Stable Video Diffusion, Tune-A-Video and Make-A-Video, while adding OpenVid and FSDP. It corrects the implementation paragraph's DMD2 citation and explains SLA's exclusion through its stated GPU-kernel restriction. The central positioning against sparse attention and intra-layer mixed attention is retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method prose receive localized rewriting, and related work is shortened. The separate Efficiency Discussion is absorbed into Main Results, the ablation subsection is renumbered, and supplementary material is organized into Appendix A–H. The main narrative and method exposition remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from a radar chart to labeled bar panels for both model sizes. Table 1 gains latency columns and model groups, while Table 2 incorporates latency information previously plotted separately. The frame-scaling plot is removed, and the appendix adds Figures I–IV and Tables I–II. V1 Figure 8 is retained as v2 Figure 6, rather than constituting a new analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important reporting deficiency: v1 repeatedly points to an absent appendix for training settings, derivation and supporting analyses. These are now inspectable, and Wan14B comparisons test the efficiency–quality tradeoff beyond the original small model. Removing the longer-video latency sweep and introducing a default-score discrepancy—26.57 in Appendix Table I versus 26.52 in the main tables—are drawbacks, but the gains in reproducibility and verifiable support are substantial.
